Good web design Portland Oregon customers respond to is not loud. It tells them what you make or fix, which part of town you are in, and how to reach you, and it does that on a phone in a few seconds. That is true for a sewing studio in an old warehouse, a roofer who covers both sides of the Columbia, and a cafe on a street that closes for a summer fair.

Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson, writing every page himself. You see a free demo of your site first, and the prices are printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, paid once.

Six address sections, not four

Portland splits its streets into named sections, and people use them in conversation. "We are in Southeast" means something to a Portlander that a ZIP code does not. For decades the city had five: North, Northeast, Northwest, Southeast and Southwest. In 2020 the city created a sixth, South Portland, out of the part of Southwest that sits east of SW Naito Parkway, or east of SW View Point Terrace farther south. About 6,000 addresses in South Waterfront, Collins View and Riverdale changed. "SW" became "S," the leading zeros came off, the Postal Service accepted old addresses for one more year, and the last Southwest street signs there were scheduled to come down in May 2025.

If your business is in that area and your website, Google Business Profile or delivery instructions still say "SW" with a leading zero, fix it. A wrong section prefix can send a driver or a first-time customer to the other side of the river.

SectionA few places owners will recognizeWhat the site should make obvious

SouthSouth Waterfront, Collins View, RiverdaleYour current address, written the new way

Portland Oregon website design for people who make things

Portland has a habit of making its own goods in small batches. Portland Made, a collective of local makers and manufacturers, was started in 2012 by Kelley Roy, founder of the ADX makerspace, to organize what was already a fast-growing movement. A 2018 Urban Manufacturing Alliance snapshot, done with Portland State University and Prosper Portland as local partners, found that the city's makers and manufacturers were growing but struggling to find affordable space inside the city.

That pressure shows up online. A maker who rents a small shared shop, sells at markets on weekends, ships to a few retailers and takes custom orders has four audiences with four different questions. The website has to answer all of them without becoming a maze.

For a shopper who met you at a market

Your name exactly as it was on the booth sign, photos of the real products, and the next place they can find you in person. Many of these visitors type your name from memory, so the site has to come up for close misspellings too.

For a shop buyer or a custom client

A plain wholesale or commission page: minimums, lead times, how to send a request, and a form that lands in your inbox. If you already sell through an outside store, the site links to it clearly. A cart is not something we build, and we say that up front.

Street fairs, studio nights and the hours around them

Some Portland neighborhoods run on events. On Alberta Street in Northeast, Last Thursday closes about fifteen blocks to traffic on summer evenings from 6 to 9 p.m., with galleries, food and artisans along the route. The Mississippi Street Fair in July draws more than 30,000 visitors to that close-in North Portland street.

Those nights bring in people who have never heard of you. The next morning some of them search for the shop they walked past. If your site shows your regular hours, your event hours and a photo of the storefront they will remember, you are easy to find again. If the site still lists last year's fair date, they move on.

Home service crews across the metro

Cleaners, painters, handymen and organizers work the whole metro, which the Census Bureau estimated at about 2.54 million people in 2024 across the Portland, Vancouver and Hillsboro area. A cleaning service in Gresham and one in Lake Oswego serve very different streets. Each site should name the towns and sections it really covers, and nothing it does not.

Web design Portland contractors need when the work crosses a river

The metro area spans two states. Vancouver, Washington is part of the same Census metro as Portland and Hillsboro, and many trades work on both sides of the Columbia, while others stay in Oregon and head west to Beaverton or east to Gresham. Google says local results depend on relevance, distance and prominence. A roofer whose site says only "serving the Portland area" gives Google little to match against a search typed in Vancouver or Hillsboro. A short, honest page for each place you truly serve does better than a long list of town names at the bottom of the home page.

For an electrician, the site carries a heavier load: what kind of work you take, whether you handle older houses, how to book an estimate, and the license details customers expect to see. We put those on the page in plain language and keep a button to call in reach on every screen.

What it costs, said once and plainly

Oregon is a small business state. The SBA Office of Advocacy's 2024 profile counts 409,958 small businesses in Oregon, 99.4% of all businesses, employing 53.5% of the state's workers. Most of those owners have no marketing staff, which is why the price and the monthly bill matter as much as the design.

  • Starter, $497 once. Five pages written for your business, a contact form that emails every lead, Google Maps and hours on the page, live in 7 to 14 days.
  • Pro, $997 once. Ten pages with a photo gallery, lead capture on every page, local SEO with Google Business Profile setup, your Google reviews on the site, and 10 city pages, each one researched and written from scratch. The AI chat widget is free for 14 days, then $297 a month if you keep it.
  • Agency, $1,997 once. Keyword research across your service area first, then a page for each town and service worth having, delivered in waves with the first live inside two weeks, plus custom design. It includes setup of an AI phone agent, which is free for 7 days and then $297 a month for up to 750 minutes, cancel any time. That monthly charge is separate from the one-time price.

Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep an AI agent; otherwise they cost $49 a month. You own the site. We do not sell page counts: a maker with six strong pages is better served than one with forty thin ones.

Portland help to use before or alongside us

  • PCC Small Business Development CenterPortland Community College runs the local SBDC, with free, confidential one-on-one advising and paid training programs. It also offers advising by appointment at the Portland Metro Chamber office.
  • Prosper PortlandThe city's economic development agency runs the Inclusive Business Resource Network, launched in 2017. It funds community organizations that give owners one-on-one advising and training, and its clients can get help with legal questions, accounting, bookkeeping and credit.
  • Portland Metro ChamberThe Portland Business Alliance took back the Portland Metro Chamber name in June 2023. The organization traces its roots to the Portland Trade Board of 1870.

Common questions

How do I choose between Portland web design companies?

Ask each one for three things in writing: the total price, what you pay every month after launch, and who owns the site and the domain when you are done. Then look at whether the pages they show you were written for a business or poured into a template. Our answers: $497, $997 or $1,997 once; $49 a month for hosting, maintenance and updates, or included while you keep an AI agent, which itself costs $297 a month after its free trial; and you own the site outright. You also see a free demo of your own site before deciding.

Is this page about Portland, Maine?

No. This page is about Portland, Oregon, on the Willamette and Columbia rivers. We can build a site for a business in Portland, Maine too, but nothing on this page describes it.

Is there affordable or freelance web design in Portland that is still written by hand?

Yes. Dominion Web Design Pro works the way a freelancer does: one person, Maurice Johnson, talks with you and writes every page himself. The difference is that the prices are fixed and printed. Starter is $497 one time for five pages and goes live in 7 to 14 days.

Can you build an online store for the products I make in Portland?

An online store with a shopping cart is not part of our packages, and we would rather say so now than surprise you later. What we do build is the site around your products: what you make, how it is made, where shoppers can buy it in person, a wholesale or custom order form, and a clear link to the store you already sell through. If you need a platform such as Shopify or WordPress, raise it when you ask for the demo.

Do you have an office in Portland, Oregon?

No. Maurice builds every site from Big Sandy, East Texas, and works with Portland owners by phone, email and shared links. Call (903) 636-7511 at any hour; an AI receptionist answers and can transfer you to Maurice.

See your website before you pay for it

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
